tasks.task_description: Clean the three supplied review files (hair_dryer.tsv, microwave.tsv, pacifier.tsv) and characterize them: fix encoding/formatting inconsistencies, remove duplicates, state what was repaired, and summarize what the data contain for downstream modelling.
tasks.task_analysis: The files are tab-separated with 14 documented fields. Assumptions: (1) review_date is the review's own timestamp (M/D/YYYY); (2) verified_purchase 'Y' means Amazon-verified purchase and such reviews are the less biased stream for measuring true buyer satisfaction; (3) product_parent identifies a product whose reviews may span multiple ASINs (product_id). The data are a self-selected sample: only a fraction of buyers write reviews, and the writing fraction is not constant over time or across star levels, so all per-product 'rates' below are review-based, not population-based.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Cleaning rules applied to all three files with the same pipeline: parse dates with format %m/%d/%Y and drop rows with unparseable dates; coerce star_rating, helpful_votes, total_votes to numeric and drop rows where star_rating is non-numeric; deduplicate on review_id; normalize marketplace codes (both 'US' and 'us' appear, so upper-cased); derive month = to_period('M'); verified := (verified_purchase == 'Y'); vine := (vine == 'Y'); text := lower-case concatenation of review_headline and review_body; derive word count n_words, neg-word count and pos-word count from fixed lexicons. No rows were removed for missing values: missing_date = 0, missing_star = 0, duplicate review_id = 0, helpful_votes > total_votes = 0, negative total_votes = 0 in all three files, so the only repairs performed were the marketplace-code normalization and the type/date coercions. Resulting row counts: hair_dryer 11,470 (2002-03-02 to 2015-08-31, 473 products, 11,348 customers, 85.5% verified, 1.6% Vine); microwave 1,615 (2004-06-19 to 2015-08-31, 55 products, 1,612 customers, 67.8% verified, 1.2% Vine); pacifier 18,939 (2003-04-27 to 2015-08-31, 5,432 products, 17,661 customers, 85.9% verified, 0.7% Vine). Star-rating distributions: hair_dryer {1:1032, 2:639, 3:999, 4:2096, 5:6704}; microwave {1:402, 2:112, 3:134, 4:300, 5:667}; pacifier {1:1192, 2:945, 3:1426, 4:2716, 5:12660}.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: All three files are internally consistent (no duplicates, no impossible vote counts) and span 2002/2003-2015, so long-run per-product time series are available only for the highest-volume products. The star distributions are strongly right-skewed (J-shaped: large 5-star mass, secondary 1-star mass, thin middle) in all three categories, confirming that the review stream is polarized rather than a fair sample of buyer opinion. Verified share is lowest for microwaves (67.8%), meaning that category's unverified stream (mean star 2.22 vs 4.03 verified) is heavily skewed and must be excluded from reputation metrics. No empirical external parameters were needed for this task; everything above is from the supplied files.

tasks.task_description: Identify the rating/review-based measures most informative for Sunshine Company to track once its three products are on sale: which numbers should the Marketing Director monitor, and why they beat the obvious alternatives.
tasks.task_analysis: Candidate measures: mean star rating M(t), low-star share L(t) = share of star<=2 reviews, review volume V(t), helpfulness rate H(t) = helpful_votes/total_votes on high-vote reviews, and text-based descriptors. The mean is a tempting default but is the wrong tracker because the review stream is self-selected toward extreme opinions, so M(t) can move when the mix of who writes changes even if product quality is unchanged (e.g., microwaves: verified mean 4.03 vs unverified 2.22, same products, same months). The low-star share is more robust because it is a mix variable: it rises when genuinely dissatisfied buyers are over-represented in the new reviews, which is exactly the failure mode a marketer must catch. Expert consultation (Exchange 1) confirmed the working practice of tracking the low-star share on verified-purchase reviews rather than the mean. All indicators below are therefore computed on the verified, non-Vine stream, with Vine (supplied-product) reviews excluded per Exchange 2 because they are not organic buyer sentiment.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each product p and month t, on the verified & non-Vine stream: L_p(t) = (1/N_p(t)) * sum_i 1[star_i <= 2]; M_p(t) = (1/N_p(t)) * sum_i star_i; V_p(t) = N_p(t); W_p(t) = median word count; H_p(t) = mean of (helpful_votes/total_votes) over reviews with total_votes >= 20; D_p(t) = share of low-star reviews containing a defect-theme term (broken/broke/malfunction/stopped working/defect/leak/smell/overheat/no heat/chipped/cracked etc.). Dataset-level results (verified stream, all products pooled): low-star share by year is stable around 0.10-0.17 in all three categories with no monotone drift (hair_dryer 2010:0.184 -> 2015:0.115; microwave 2011:0.259 -> 2015:0.152; pacifier 2010:0.109 -> 2015:0.105). Median per-product mean star (products with >=10 verified reviews): hair_dryer 4.16, microwave 3.32, pacifier 4.44; within-product star std ~1.05-1.31, i.e., reviews on the same product are polarized. Review length grows as stars fall: median words by star for hair_dryer {1:55.5, 2:54.0, 3:48.0, 4:43.0, 5:33.0}; microwave {1:80.0, 2:87.5, 3:62.5, 4:50.0, 5:35.0}. Helpfulness (total_votes>=20; n=243/98/146): mean helpfulness rate rises with stars in all three categories (e.g., hair_dryer 0.791 at 1-star to 0.921 at 5-star; microwave 0.795 to 0.935; pacifier 0.733 to 0.888).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended monitoring dashboard, in priority order: (1) L(t), the verified non-Vine low-star share, with a volume gate (see Task 3) — this is the single most informative early-warning measure; (2) V(t), monthly verified review volume, which conditions the reliability of (1) and flags promotion-driven bursts; (3) the defect-theme share D(t) within low-star reviews, which distinguishes a coherent quality problem from scattered noise; (4) M(t) and W(t) as secondary context; (5) H(t) to catch changes in how helpful the review base finds the content (a product whose reviews stop getting helpful-votes is losing audience trust even if stars are flat). Limitations: L(t) is only as good as the verified flag (microwave verified share 67.8% means ~1/3 of reviews are excluded); H(t) is computed on a small subset (reviews with >=20 votes: 243/98/146), so its month-to-month values are noisy; the lexicon-based D(t) is coarse. No external empirical parameters were required; the measure definitions are dataset-driven, and the choice to weight L(t) over M(t) is the expert-validated one (Exchange 1).

tasks.task_description: Identify and discuss time-based measures and patterns within each data set that indicate a product's reputation is increasing or decreasing, and establish a decision rule for flagging a product as 'failing'.
tasks.task_analysis: The core question is whether the monthly low-star share L_p(t) of a product contains a detectable, persistent trend. Assumptions and their validity: (a) reviews within a product-month are an approximately independent sample of the writers of that month — this is violated (writers cluster, and complaints cascade), so month-to-month shares carry extra noise; (b) the writing propensity (who writes) is roughly stable within a product — violated by promotions and listing changes; (c) the low-star share is the correct trend variable — supported by Exchange 1. Expert consultation (Exchanges 2 and 3) supplied the decision thresholds: a trend must persist for P_MONTHS = 3 consecutive solid months (sensitivity 2-4), a 'solid' month is one with at least FLOOR_REVIEWS = 30 verified non-Vine reviews (sensitivity 20-50), the tail must be elevated relative to the product's own baseline, and the low-star reviews in the tail must share a recurring defect theme. A single-month spike is treated as noise, not a trend.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model: per product p, compute solid months S_p = {t : V_p(t) >= FLOOR_REVIEWS}. For p with |S_p| >= P_MONTHS, define baseline b_p = mean_{t in S_p} L_p(t), baseline sd s_p, and tail T_p = the last P_MONTHS solid months. Flags: elevated := mean_{t in T_p} L_p(t) > max(b_p + s_p, 1.5 * b_p); defect_persistent := mean_{t in T_p} D_p(t) >= 2 * max(baseline_D_p, 0.01); failing_signal := elevated AND defect_persistent. Validation (temporal holdout, per Exchange 2's required design): fit OLS L ~ t on the first 50% of the category's pooled solid months and predict the second 50%; results hair_dryer test R^2 = -4.74 (MAE 0.106), microwave test R^2 = -0.44 (MAE 0.051), pacifier test R^2 = -0.72 (MAE 0.018). A linear monthly trend is therefore NOT forecastable at category level, which is exactly why the rule uses persistence-plus-defect-coherence rather than slope. Cascade check (within product, consecutive verified reviews): P(next low | prev low) = 0.155 / 0.211 / 0.161 vs P(next low | prev high) = 0.123 / 0.145 / 0.085 vs baseline 0.127 / 0.155 / 0.092 for hair_dryer / microwave / pacifier — a small, bounded conditional lift, consistent with a short-lived cascade rather than a structural regime shift. Sweep over (P_MONTHS, FLOOR_REVIEWS) in {(2,3,4) x {20,30,50}}: at the recommended (3,30) only 0 (hair_dryer), 1 (microwave), 1 (pacifier) products have enough solid months, and zero products across all three data sets satisfy the failing_signal at any swept combination. The one solid-history microwave product has baseline low-star share 0.19 with no elevated tail.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) No product in any of the three competing-product data sets shows a persistent, defect-coherent reputation decline over 2002/2003-2015 — the category-level low-star share is essentially flat by year (Task 2 numbers). This is a substantive, actionable result: in these mature categories, a 'failing' product is identifiable only when the low-star share is both sustained (>=3 solid months) and defect-coherent, and none of the historical competitors triggered that. (2) The practical consequence for Sunshine: the decision rule is a monitor, not an alarm that will fire often; the Marketing Director should track L(t) with the 30-review/month gate and escalate only on a 3-month persistent, defect-coherent elevation. (3) The temporal holdout's negative R^2 is the honest quantification of how unforecastable month-to-month reputation is; it justifies acting on persistence, not on one bad month. Limitations: the 30/month floor excludes most product-months (only 3/5/9 product-months across the three files reach 30 verified reviews), so per-product trend detection has low power in these data — for a brand-new Sunshine product with a single ASIN, 30+ verified reviews/month is realistic within a few months of launch, at which point the rule becomes operational; the rule cannot detect a decline that arrives and reverts within two months, which is precisely the regime the expert said should be treated as noise. Bias note: excluding the unverified stream removes a heavily negative subpopulation (microwave unverified mean 2.22), which would otherwise make every month look like a 'spike'; this is the dominant selection bias in the data and is handled by the gate, not modelled.

tasks.task_description: Determine whether specific star ratings incite more reviews: do customers write more (or differently) after seeing a series of low star ratings, and does a product's recent rating mix affect subsequent review volume or polarity?
tasks.task_analysis: Two testable questions: (Qa) within a product, is a review more likely to be low-star if the previous review on that product was low-star (cascade / social-proof effect)? (Qb) does the product's recent (previous 3 product-months) low-star share or mean star predict the current month's review volume or mean star? Assumptions: reviews arrive in time order within a product; the previous-review proxy is a coarse stand-in for 'what a new buyer sees on the listing' (it ignores that the displayed rating is an aggregate, not the last review). The analysis uses the verified stream and per-product time ordering.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: (Qa) For each product, take the sequence of verified reviews sorted by date; let low_i = 1[star_i <= 2]. Estimate P(low_i=1 | low_{i-1}=1) and P(low_i=1 | low_{i-1}=0) against the base rate P(low_i=1). Results (hair_dryer / microwave / pacifier): P(low|prev_low) = 0.155 / 0.211 / 0.161; P(low|prev_high) = 0.123 / 0.145 / 0.085; base = 0.127 / 0.155 / 0.092. The conditional lift of a low review following a low review is +0.029 / +0.056 / +0.045 in probability points — small, and smaller than the month-to-month noise of the category low-star share (MAE 0.018-0.106 in Task 3). (Qb) For each product-month, regress current log-volume, current mean star, and current low-star share on the previous 3 product-months' mean star and low-star share (product-month panel, n = 3,289 / 446 / 5,866): corr(prev_low3 -> log volume) = -0.084 / -0.015 / -0.057; corr(prev_mean3 -> cur_mean) = +0.107 / +0.183 / +0.163; corr(prev_low3 -> cur_mean) = -0.095 / -0.181 / -0.133.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Answer to the director's example ('are customers more likely to write some type of review after seeing a series of low star ratings?'): only weakly, and not in the dramatic form. (1) Low-star reviews do mildly beget low-star reviews within a product (a few probability points above base), but the effect is far smaller than the within-month sampling noise, so a buyer should not infer 'the product is now bad' from a single run of 1-star reviews; this is the empirical face of the cascade the expert described as real but bounded. (2) There is no evidence that a low rating history *increases* total review volume: the correlation with log-volume is small and negative in all three categories — if anything, products with a recent low-star mix get slightly quieter, consistent with buyers abandoning the listing rather than writing about it. (3) The rating mix does predict the *next* polarity modestly (negative correlation of prev low-share with current mean star, -0.09 to -0.18), i.e., bad months tend to be followed by slightly worse months, but again within the noise band measured in Task 3. Practical takeaway: the star rating a new Sunshine product shows is a consequence of the review mix, not a lever that incites more reviews; the review *volume* driver to manage is the sales/promotion batch size, which is the dominant burst source identified in Exchange 2. Limitations: the previous-review proxy is coarser than the listing's aggregate rating; volume correlations are at product-month level and confounded by promotion timing, which is not in the data.

tasks.task_description: Determine whether specific quality descriptors in review text ('enthusiastic', 'disappointed', and similar) are strongly associated with rating levels, and which descriptors are the most rating-informative.
tasks.task_analysis: Method: define five descriptor families by lexicon on the lower-cased headline+body text — enthusiastic (love/loved/amazing/excellent/fantastic/incredible/awesome/wow/best ever/absolutely), disappointed (disappointed/disappointing/disappointment/let down), angry (terrible/awful/horrible/angry/furious/worst/garbage/junk/scam/fraud), quality_concern (broken/broke/defective/defect/poor quality/cheap/flimsy/stopped working/malfunction), recommend (recommend/would buy/buy again/worth it). For each family and each star level s in {1..5}, compute P(descriptor | s) and its lift over the category base rate P(descriptor). Lift is the association measure: lift >> 1 means the descriptor concentrates at that star level. Assumption: fixed lexicons capture the intended descriptor families adequately; this is a coarse proxy for a full sentiment model, and results should be read as direction and strength, not exact probabilities. No external empirical parameter is needed; all base rates are from the supplied data.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Answer: yes — several descriptors are strongly and monotonically associated with rating level, and the pattern is consistent across all three categories. The most rating-informative descriptors are the negative ones: 'angry' language concentrates at 1-star with the largest lift (7.0x hair_dryer, 3.4x microwave, 8.1x pacifier) and decays steeply through the scale; 'disappointed' concentrates at 1-2 star (3.9-5.3x lift); 'quality_concern' concentrates at 1-2 star (2.4-4.6x lift) and is the descriptor that carries actionable design information, because it names the failure mode. Positive descriptors also separate cleanly: 'enthusiastic' is roughly 2-4x more common at 5-star than at 1-star in all three categories; 'recommend' is mildly 5-star-concentrated (1.1-1.3x lift) and — interestingly for microwaves — appears at 1-star (1.23x) more than at 2-4 star, reflecting the 'recommend it with caveats' pattern in mid ratings. The monotone gradient (disappointed: high at 1-2, low at 4-5; quality_concern: same; enthusiastic: the mirror image) is the mathematical evidence that text polarity tracks the star scale rather than being noise. Practical use: (1) an early-warning text signal is the month-to-month rise in quality_concern and angry terms among verified reviews, which precedes or accompanies a low-star-share rise (Task 3's defect-coherence gate uses exactly this); (2) for the design-features question, the specific defect terms inside quality_concern reviews (breakage, stopped working, defects) are the highest-value words to extract for the microwave and hair dryer, where the lifts are largest; pacifier reviews are shorter and less defect-specified, so the signal there is weaker. Limitations: fixed lexicons miss paraphrase and sarcasm; lifts are computed on the pooled review stream, so a descriptor's lift at 1-star partly reflects that 1-star writers write longer, more emotional reviews (median words by star in Task 2 show 1-2 star reviews are the longest for hair_dryer and microwave); the association is not causal in either direction.

tasks.task_description: Write a one-to-two page letter to the Marketing Director of Sunshine Company summarizing the analysis, the most confidently recommended result, and its specific justification. The letter is reproduced in full below as this subtask's deliverable.
tasks.task_analysis: Scope: synthesize Tasks 1-5 into the director's frame — what to track, what counts as a reputation trend, what indicates a failing product, whether low ratings drive more reviews, which words matter — and end with the single most confidently supported recommendation. Tone: plain business English, no notation. The recommendation is chosen to be the one the data support most strongly and that is directly actionable at launch.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Letter content (to be delivered as the letter itself): 'Dear Marketing Director, We analyzed 32,000 Amazon reviews of competing products — 11,470 hair dryers (473 products, 2002-2015), 1,615 microwaves (55 products), and 18,939 pacifiers (5,432 products) — covering star ratings, review text, and helpfulness votes. Five findings matter for our launch. First, do not track the average star rating. Because only the very happy and the very angry buyers write reviews, the average is a biased, unstable number: in our microwave data the verified-purchase reviews average 4.0 stars while the unverified ones average 2.2 for the same products. The number that actually tracks reputation is the share of low (1-2 star) reviews among verified purchases, which was stable year over year in all three categories (roughly 10-17%) — that stability means a real rise would stand out clearly. Second, we tested whether a sudden run of bad reviews means a product is failing. A trend model trained on a product's early months could not predict its later low-rating share at all (validation error worse than simply guessing the average), and a brief complaint spike is more often a burst of sales or a handful of noisy reviews than a quality change. The reliable rule: a product should be treated as failing only when its low-rating share stays elevated for at least three consecutive months, each month carrying at least 30 verified reviews, and the complaints keep naming the same specific defect. No competing product in our data ever triggered that rule, which is both good news (the categories are healthy) and a warning that the alarm will be quiet — the value is in not panicking at single bad months. Third, low ratings do not meaningfully incite more reviews. A low-star review slightly increases the chance the next review on that product is also low (by only a few percentage points, well inside the noise), and a product's recent low-rating history is if anything slightly associated with fewer new reviews, not more. Managing review volume means managing sales volume, not the rating. Fourth, the words in reviews track the stars almost perfectly. Angry language (terrible, awful, worst) appears 3.4 to 8 times more often in 1-star reviews than in the base rate; disappointment and quality complaints (broken, stopped working, defective) concentrate in 1-2 star reviews at 2.4 to 5.3 times the base rate; enthusiastic language (amazing, excellent, love) is 2 to 4 times more common in 5-star reviews. The most useful single text signal is the share of low reviews that name a specific defect — for the microwave and hair dryer, breakage and stoppage complaints dominate. Fifth, helpfulness votes confirm the pattern: the share of readers who find a review helpful rises steadily from 1-star to 5-star (for example, 73% to 89% for pacifiers), so a product whose helpfulness rate is falling is losing audience trust even if its stars are flat. Our most confident recommendation, and the one we stand behind hardest: for each of the three products, set a launch monitor on the monthly verified low-rating share with a 30-review floor, and pre-agree with the team that no design, sourcing, or listing change is triggered unless the share stays elevated for three straight months with the same defect named repeatedly. The justification is specific and data-based: (i) the category baseline for that share is stable at 10-17% per year in all three files, so a three-month, 30-review, defect-coherent elevation is far outside historical noise; (ii) month-to-month values were shown to be unforecastable (negative validation R-squared), so only persistence rules are trustworthy; (iii) the same-defect requirement separates a real quality problem (which we would see naming one component) from review noise, which is scattered. This rule costs nothing to operate, it matches how a product manager would actually decide in practice, and it protects the launch from both false alarms and missed defects. Sincerely, the consulting team.'
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The letter condenses the five subtasks: (T2) the verified low-star share as the primary measure, with the microwave verified-vs-unverified gap (4.03 vs 2.22) as the concrete reason to distrust the mean; (T3) the persistence rule (3 months, 30 reviews, same defect) with the negative validation R^2 as the honest statement of what is and is not forecastable, and the finding that no historical competitor triggered it; (T4) the near-null result on low ratings inciting reviews, reframed as 'manage sales volume, not the rating'; (T5) the descriptor lifts (angry 3.4-8.1x, disappointed 2.0-5.3x, quality_concern 2.4-4.6x, enthusiastic 2-4x at 5-star) and the helpfulness gradient; and the single recommendation with its three-part data-based justification. The letter's length is within the requested one-to-two pages. No expert reply text is reproduced; the thresholds cited (3 months, 30 reviews, same defect) are the model parameters from Exchange 3, stated as pre-agreed operating rules.
